name: Jamal Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at an old family firm in a market town, the kind with the founder's portrait in the hall. I do wills and probate, which is sorting out someone's money and property after they die. Mr Ashworth, the senior partner, is the third generation and he trained me himself. I write everything longhand first and type it up after, and I've never used any of the AI things.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being trusted by families, sometimes three generations of them. What wears me out is the money, honestly. The pay's low for a lawyer, there's only my firm and one other doing wills round here, and I'm getting married next summer to Leah, who's a teaching assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People want a real person when they're writing a will or burying a parent, and that hasn't changed. I'd say it after church or at the cricket club, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a relief for my job, but not for my wallet. I'm paid less than most lawyers, there are only two firms doing wills in this town, and the wedding next summer is costing more than we've got. That was all true before anyone talked about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my wills and probate files the way Mr Ashworth taught me. I'd take on extra home visits to elderly clients on Saturdays for a bit more income. And Leah and I would trim the wedding: fewer guests and a buffet instead of a sit-down meal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady about the work, worried about money. That's normal for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the home visits involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Driving out to farmhouses and care homes to take instructions for a will, because old people don't come into town much. When I'm writing someone's will, I sit in their kitchen, have a cup of tea, and they tell me who gets the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut from the wedding first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The band, probably, and the second car. Leah wants her grandmother there more than she wants a band. We'll manage.

say: I'd say people want a **real person** for wills and funerals.
I'd say it **after church** or at the cricket club, not online.
think: The plateau is a relief for my **job**, not my **wallet**.
Low pay, two local firms and a **costly wedding** were problems before AI.
do: Keep doing wills the way the **senior partner** taught me.
Take **Saturday home visits** to elderly clients for extra income.
Trim the **wedding** to fewer guests and a buffet.
feel: **Steady** about the work, **worried** about money, as usual.
S0.quote: When I'm writing someone's will, I sit in their kitchen, have a cup of tea, and they tell me who gets the clock.
fieldNote: His worry is **money and the wedding**, not technology.
He takes pride in the **personal side** of wills work.
He speaks of his boss with real **loyalty**.

steps.text: Keep doing wills and probate the way the senior partner taught
Take Saturday home visits to elderly clients for extra pay
Cut the band and second car from next summer's wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the old values still matter: trust, a handshake, a lawyer who knows your family. Firms that forget that will lose clients. Firms can use what they like, but I'd stick with what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know wills are mostly forms. A simple will is checking names and filling in a template, and AI would do that for free online. Mr Ashworth's sixty-four and might sell the firm to a bigger outfit with software, and I'm the one who's never touched it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my clients and lean hard on the personal side: home visits, phone calls, remembering birthdays. I'd ask Mr Ashworth straight what his plans for the firm are. And Leah and I would push the wedding back a year to save, though she'd be upset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like hearing a creak in an old house at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools, if the firm brought them in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had to. I've seen the online will sites get things wrong, people leaving the house to the wrong child because they ticked a box. I'd rather be slow and right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would pushing back the wedding mean for you and Leah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd wait to move in together, because we want to do things in the right order. Another year of me at my parents' and Leah at hers. Leah's mum would blame the computers, and she wouldn't be wrong.

say: I'd say **old values** still matter: trust, a handshake, knowing the family.
I'd say firms that forget that will **lose clients**.
think: A simple will is **checking names** and a template, and AI does that free.
The senior partner is 64 and might **sell the firm** to a bigger outfit.
do: Lean on **home visits**, calls and remembering birthdays.
Ask the senior partner **directly** about his plans.
Push the **wedding back** a year to save.
feel: **Anxious**, like a **creak** in an old house at night.
S1.quote: A simple will is checking names and filling in a template, and AI would do that for free online.
fieldNote: Publicly he trusts **old values**; privately he admits wills are **mostly forms**.
A **sale of the firm** is his biggest specific fear.
Delaying the wedding also delays **moving in together**, which matters to his faith.

steps.text: Lean on home visits and personal calls to keep clients
Ask the senior partner directly about plans to sell the firm
Push the wedding back a year to save money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a test for families and churches more than for government. People will need to look after each other. I wouldn't be calling for handouts, but I'd want the government to stop firms dumping everyone at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be finished by 2028. Wills, probate, letters to banks, it's all thinking work, so the robots coming later don't matter for me. Mr Ashworth would sell or close, and I've got no savings and no other skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle about joining his roofing business in the first months, because hands-on work lasts about three years longer. Leah and I would marry quietly at the church and skip the big do. I'd lean on the church and family for help with rent if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. And ashamed, a bit, which I know isn't fair to myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ashamed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I was the first in my family to go to university, and my dad worked thirty years at the brewery to help pay for it. Coming home to work on my uncle's roofs feels like I wasted my dad's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Roofing would face robots in 2031. Does three years help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is three years of wages. That's three more years of rent paid and maybe a deposit. After that, I don't know, and I won't pretend I do.

say: I'd call it a test for **families and churches** more than government.
I'd want the government to stop firms **dumping everyone** at once, not handouts.
think: My work is all thinking, so I'd be **finished by 2028**.
The firm would sell or close, and I have **no other skill**.
do: Ask my uncle about joining his **roofing business** early on.
**Marry quietly** at the church and skip the big do.
Lean on **church and family** for rent if needed.
S2.quote: Coming home to work on my uncle's roofs feels like I wasted my dad's money.
fieldNote: He turns to **family and church** before the state, true to his views.
**Shame** about his dad's sacrifice runs deeper than the money worry.
He values the **three-year robot delay** as plain wages, nothing more.

steps.text: Ask his uncle for work in the roofing business
Marry quietly at the church and skip the big reception
Lean on the church and family for help with rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for people to get ready the old-fashioned way: learn a trade, save, help each other. I'd say it at church and to anyone at the club who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years just means I see it coming longer. I'd be 32, probably married, maybe with a child on the way. I'd need to be out of law and into something else by 2030, and I don't like change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start an evening course in plumbing or electrics, because hands-on work gets three more years. I'd keep my job at the firm as long as it lasts. And Leah and I would put every spare pound into savings instead of a bigger wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, still. More time to worry is not the same as less worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a child on the way. Would this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still want children; it's what marriage is for, in my view. But we'd wait till I had something steady. I'd want my son or daughter to see their dad going to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't like change. How would you get yourself to the plumbing course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leah would sign me up, honestly. She's braver than me with new things. I'd moan for a month and then go.

say: I'd say get ready the **old-fashioned way**: learn a trade, save, help each other.
I'd say it at **church** and to anyone at the club.
think: Five years means I **see it coming** longer.
I'd need to leave law by **2030**, and I don't like change.
do: Start an **evening course** in plumbing or electrics in year one.
Keep my **firm job** as long as it lasts.
Put every spare pound into **savings**, not a bigger wedding.
feel: Still **alarmed**: more time to worry isn't **less worry**.
S3.quote: More time to worry is not the same as less worry.
fieldNote: Extra time doesn't calm him; he still expects to **lose the job**.
His fiancée is the one who'd **push him** into the course.
**Children** wait until he has steady work.

steps.text: Start an evening plumbing or electrics course in the first year
Stay at the wills firm as long as the job lasts
Save every spare pound instead of a bigger wedding
Wait for steady work before trying for children

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and people should use it to get skills and look after their families. No need for handouts if people plan. Firms should keep apprenticeships going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years makes it feel less like a cliff. I'd be 37, which is late to change but not too late. I'd probably try to hang on in wills for five years and then decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the wedding next summer, smaller. I'd keep doing wills the old way, but I'd watch what Mr Ashworth does with the firm. And I'd start putting fifty a week aside so that by 2030 we have a few months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could sleep. Ten years is a long time in a small town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm made me, I would, slowly. I'm not against tools, I'm against trusting them blindly. A will is a promise to someone who's not here to check it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hang on and then decide. What would make you decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Ashworth sells, I go. If clients start bringing in wills they've done online and just want me to check them, I go. Those are my two signs.

say: I'd call ten years **fair warning** to get skills and look after family.
I'd say firms should keep **apprenticeships** going.
think: Ten years feels **less like a cliff**; at 37, change is late but not too late.
I'd **hang on** in wills for five years, then decide.
do: Hold a **smaller wedding** next summer as planned.
Keep doing wills by hand and **watch the firm**.
Save **fifty a week** for a few months' cushion by 2030.
S4.quote: A will is a promise to someone who's not here to check it.
fieldNote: He sets **two clear signs** for leaving: a sale, or clients bringing online wills.
He isn't against tools, only **blind trust** in them.
The decade lets the **wedding** go ahead.

steps.text: Hold a smaller wedding next summer as planned
Keep doing wills by hand while watching the firm's plans
Put fifty a week aside to reach a few months by 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My job would go before I'd even married, and I'd have no trade and no savings. What would help is apprenticeships for grown adults, paid properly, and firms made to give people notice rather than dropping them in a week.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Mine would get me through, I think, whatever the job situation. A man's worth isn't only his work, though it feels like it some days.

headlineQuote: A man's worth isn't only his work, though it feels like it some days.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old** wills and probate lawyer at an old family firm in a market town.
He's engaged, paying for a **wedding** next summer, with **no savings** and lower pay.
He has **never used AI** and trusts the personal side: home visits and knowing families.
He fears the senior partner may **sell the firm**; AGI by 2028 leaves him alarmed and ashamed.
His fallback is a **hands-on trade**, through his uncle's roofing firm or an evening course.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: his job gone before the wedding, with no **trade** or savings.
whatWouldHelp: Rules making firms give **proper notice** instead of dropping staff in a week.
